newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel-Fosamax OK to prevent osteoporosis.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel-Fosamax OK to prevent osteoporosis.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory committee unanimously recommended on Thursday that Merck and Co's Fosamax (alendronate sodium) be approved as a treatment to prevent osteoporosis in post-menopausal women and to prevent fractures in women who already have the condition.
Twenty-five to 28 million Americans, primarily women, have osteoporosis, which causes bones to become thin and brittle.
Fosamax is the first alternative to the recommended preventive treatment, estrogen replacement therapy, which many women cannot take or don't want to take because of perceived cancer risk.
HKS and Co. analyst Hemant Shah said that Fosamax could become a multi-billion dollar seller if Merck can convince women that they need to take the drug.
Osteoporosis is largely undiagnosed until patients experience fractures. Risk factors include early menopause, thin build, maternal history, and Asian or Caucasian race.
The main way to determine osteoporosis -- bone density measurement -- is not widely accessible or used, and the testing is not fully reimbursed by Medicare.
As a result, FDA panel members tried to spell out which patients should get the therapy and when to begin.
Panelists emphasized that estrogen replacement should be considered first, and that Fosamax is an option, not a cure-all.

"This is in no way a substitute" for other preventive practices such as calcium supplements, exercise, and changes in diet," said Dr. Robert Marcus of the Veterans Administration Medical Center in Palo Alto, Calif.

"Since not all women are able or willing to take estrogen replacement therapy, it would clearly be beneficial for post-menopausal women to have therapeutic choices for the prevention of osteoporosis," said Sandra Raymond, executive director of the National Osteoporosis Foundation.
Merck presented two-year data from an ongoing six-year trial, the Early Post-Menopausal Intervention Cohort.
Women were assigned to take either 2.5 mg. daily or five mg. daily of Fosamax, hormone replacement therapy, or a placebo.
The 2.5 mg. dose had little effect, but women taking the five mg. dose had bone mineral density (BMD) increases of 3.46 percent in the spine and 1.85 percent in the hip.
Hormone therapy increased BMD by 4.04 percent in the spine and 1.83 percent in the hip.
The spine, hip, and forearm are the three most common areas of fracture in osteoporosis.
In another study, the Fracture Intervention Trial, Merck showed that the drug can help prevent fractures in women who already have osteoporosis.
Women taking five mg. daily had a 51 percent reduction in hip fracture risk, a 47 percent reduction in spinal fracture risk and a 48 percent reduction in forearm fracture risk.
Data from both trials have previously been published or presented at scientific meetings.
An FDA reviewer agreed that Merck had shown that Fosamax increases bone density, helping to prevent osteoporosis.
He noted that in one study, six months after stopping therapy, patients began losing bone density.
Merck is recommending a five mg. daily dose, and panel members agreed that it was an appropriate dose.
The FDA approved Fosamax for use in the United States in September 1995 to treat both post-menopausal osteoporosis and Paget's Disease, a bone disorder.
About 1.5 million patients have taken the drug, which is sold in 49 countries.
In 1996, global Fosamax sales were $282 million, primarily in the United States.
